source_text:
Ἴδωμεν τὸ παράδοξον σημεῖον τὸ γινόμενον ἐν τοῖς ἀνατολικοῖς τόποις, τουτέστιν τοῖς περὶ τὴν Ἀραβίαν.
ὄρνεον γάρ ἐστιν, ὃ προσονομάζεται φοῖνιξ: τοῦτο μονογενὲς ὑπάρχον ζῇ ἔτη πεντακόσια, γενόμενόν τε ἤδη πρὸς ἀπόλυσιν τοῦ ἀποθανεῖν αὐτό, σηκὸν ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖ ἐκ λιβάνου καὶ σμύρνης καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀρωμάτων, εἰς ὃν πληρωθέντος τοῦ χρόνου εἰσέρχεται καὶ τελευτᾷ.
σηπομένης δὲ τῆς σαρκὸς σκώληξ τις γεννᾶται, ὃς ἐκ τῆς ἰκμάδος τοῦ τετελευτηκότος ζώου ἀνατρεφόμενος πτεροφυεῖ: εἶτα γενναῖος γενόμενος αἴρει τὸν σηκὸν ἐκεῖνον, ὅπου τὰ ὀστᾶ τοῦ προγεγονότος ἐστίν, καὶ ταῦτα βαστάζων διανύει ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀραβικῆς χώρας ἕως τῆς Αἰγύπτου εἰς τὴν λεγομένην Ἡλιούπολιν,
καὶ ἡμέρας, βλεπόντων πάντων, ἐπιπτὰς ἐπὶ τὸν τοῦ ἡλίου βωμὸν τίθησιν αὐτὰ καὶ οὕτως εἰς τοὐπίσω ἀφορμᾷ.
οἱ οὖν ἱερεῖς ἐπισκέπτονται τὰς ἀναγραφὰς τῶν χρόνων καὶ εὑρίσκουσιν αὐτὸν πεντακοσιοστοῦ ἔτους πεπληρωμένου ἐληλυθέναι.
thought_title: The Phoenix as a Sign of Resurrection
orientation: Clement is giving examples from nature that point to resurrection, and now turns to the story of the phoenix in Arabia.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see the strange sign that happens in the eastern regions, that is, the regions around Arabia. For there is a bird, which is called phoenix; this one, being only-begotten, lives five hundred years, and when it has already come to the dissolution of its dying, it makes for itself a nest from frankincense and myrrh and the remaining spices, into which, when the time has been fulfilled, it enters and dies. And when the flesh has rotted, a certain worm is born, which, being nourished from the moisture of the dead animal, grows wings; then, having become strong, it takes up that nest, where the bones of the former one are, and carrying these it travels from the Arabian country as far as Egypt to the so-called Heliopolis, and by day, while all are watching, having flown upon the altar of the sun it places them there and so departs back. The priests therefore examine the records of the times and find that it has come when the five hundredth year has been fulfilled.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of παράδοξον as 'contrary to expectation' and σημεῖον as 'sign,' matching the author's argument that this is a pointer to resurrection.
Literal rendering of μονογενής, emphasizing the bird's uniqueness; the same word is used of Christ elsewhere, so keeping it literal preserves the resonance.

choices.english: to the dissolution of its dying
choices.why: ἀπόλυσις means 'release' or 'dissolution'; rendering it literally as 'dissolution' keeps the physical sense of the body's breaking down at death.
The word can mean 'enclosure' or 'sacred precinct,' but in this natural-history context 'nest' is the plain sense of the structure the bird builds.
The verb πτεροφυέω means literally 'to put forth feathers/wings'; rendering it as 'grows wings' keeps the vivid physical process.
γενναῖος here means 'vigorous, strong' rather than 'noble'; 'strong' fits the context of the worm now able to carry the nest.

pass_b_english: Let us consider the strange sign that takes place in the eastern regions, that is, in the parts around Arabia.

There is a bird there called the phoenix. It is the only one of its kind, and it lives five hundred years. When the time of its death has drawn near, it makes for itself a nest of frankincense, myrrh, and the remaining spices. When the time is fulfilled, it enters the nest and dies.

As the flesh decays, a worm is born. Nourished by the moisture of the dead creature, the worm grows wings. Then, when it has become strong, it takes up that nest where the bones of the former bird are. Carrying them, it travels from the land of Arabia to Egypt, to the city called Heliopolis.
In daylight, while all watch, it flies to the altar of the sun and places them there. Then it turns back.
The priests then examine the records of the times and find that it has come when the five hundredth year has been completed.

polish.changed: I broke long sentences into shorter, clearer ones, made the subject of each action explicit, and reordered clauses so the sequence of events is easier to follow aloud.
Clarified the phoenix as the subject throughout, smoothed sentence flow, and made the sequence of the bird's actions easier to follow for a modern reader.
